prompt: Why did one task of the join read all 960,905 of the crawler's events?
hint: How does a shuffle choose a partition for a row?

choices.text: The crawler's events were all in one file
choices.why: They are spread over every day's file.

choices.text: They share one key, and one key hashes to one partition
choices.why: Right. The hash cannot split a single value.

choices.text: Spark sends the largest key to the first task
choices.why: The partition comes from the key's hash, not its size.

choices.text: Adaptive execution merged all of its partitions into one
choices.why: Adaptive execution was off in skew.py.

prompt: Why does speculative execution not rescue a stage held up by a skewed partition?
hint: What would the copy of the task have to read?

choices.text: A copy has the same data to get through
choices.why: Right. The task is slow because of its data, not its machine.

choices.text: Speculation is switched off for joins
choices.why: It applies to any stage.

choices.text: The copy would overwrite the first task's output
choices.why: Spark keeps whichever finishes first.

choices.text: Copies are only launched for map tasks
choices.why: Reduce tasks can be copied too.

prompt: The median task read 123,862 rows and the largest 1,086,798. How many times the median did the largest read? Round to the nearest whole number.
hint: Divide.

prompt: Which of these commonly make a hot key? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three kinds were named.

choices.text: A crawler or monitoring check
choices.why: Yes. That is `v0000000`.

choices.text: One very large customer
choices.why: Yes. The data is right and the distribution is the business.

choices.text: A key stored as a string rather than a number
choices.why: The type does not change how many rows share a value.

choices.text: A `NULL` or `unknown` written where a value was missing
choices.why: Yes. Every row with nothing to say shares it.

prompt: The hot key is a crawler whose events no report needs. What is the simplest cure?
hint: Do the rows belong in the job at all?

choices.text: Salt the join key with eight values
choices.why: That works, and costs a copy of the small side for rows nobody wants.

choices.text: Filter its rows out before the join
choices.why: Right. The skew goes with the rows.

choices.text: Raise `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` to 2,000
choices.why: One key still lands in one partition.

choices.text: Give the executors more memory
choices.why: The task stays as long as before.

prompt: Match each join strategy to what it moves.
hint: Two of them shuffle both sides.

pairs.right: The small side, whole, to every executor
Both sides by key, then a sort of each partition
Both sides by key, then a hash table per partition

right_distractors: Nothing: each side stays where it was read

prompt: Why is the sort-merge join Spark's default for two large tables?
hint: What happens when a partition is bigger than memory?

choices.text: Its sort spills to disk, so no side must fit in memory
choices.why: Right. A hash table has nowhere to go when it is too big.

choices.text: It moves fewer rows across the network than any other
choices.why: It shuffles both sides; a broadcast moves far less.

choices.text: It needs no shuffle on either side
choices.why: It shuffles both.

choices.text: It is the only one that handles a range condition
choices.why: Range-only joins use a nested loop.

prompt: In the DataFrame API, `clicks.join(F.___(books), "book_id")` asks Spark to copy the books to every task.
hint: The strategy's own name.

prompt: The planner broadcast the visitors when the query used only `visitor_id`, and not when it also used `first_day`. Why?
hint: What does it scale its size estimate by?

choices.text: Dates cannot be held in a broadcast hash table
choices.why: Any column can.

choices.text: A join with a second condition cannot be broadcast
choices.why: Extra conditions are applied after the match.

choices.text: Adaptive execution switched it back
choices.why: Both plans were the planner's first ones.

choices.text: The extra column pushed the size estimate over 10 MB
choices.why: Right. The estimate is scaled to the columns used.

prompt: Why does a broadcast join not suffer from the crawler?
hint: Where do the crawler's events stay?

choices.text: It drops keys with more than a million rows
choices.why: No join drops matching rows.

choices.text: The crawler fits in the driver
choices.why: The visitors are what is broadcast, not the events.

choices.text: The large side is never shuffled by key
choices.why: Right. Each task joins the rows it read against the whole table.

choices.text: It salts every key automatically before the join
choices.why: It needs no salt, because there is no shuffle on that side.

prompt: Where must a broadcast side fit in memory? Choose all that apply.
hint: It is paid for twice.

choices.text: In the driver, which collects it and builds the table
choices.why: Yes. That is where too_big.py failed.

choices.text: In the history server
choices.why: It only reads event logs.

choices.text: In the master, which hands it to the workers
choices.why: The master hands out cores, not data.

choices.text: In every executor, which keeps a whole copy
choices.why: Yes, for as long as the join runs.

prompt: A nightly job fails with "Not enough memory to build and broadcast the table" after a hint. What is the fix?
hint: Which way out keeps the other broadcasts?

choices.text: Set `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` to -1 for the whole cluster
choices.why: It switches off the broadcasts that were helping.

choices.text: Raise `spark.sql.broadcastTimeout`
choices.why: The failure was memory, not time.

choices.text: Double `spark.driver.memory` and run it again
choices.why: It moves the wall without removing it.

choices.text: Replace that hint with `hint("merge")`
choices.why: Right. It fixes the one join and leaves the rest alone.

prompt: A visitors table of 1.7 million rows is salted with 8 values for every visitor. How many million rows does the salted visitors side have?
hint: One copy per salt.

prompt: Why is the salt taken from a hash of `event_id` rather than from `rand()`?
hint: What happens when a task is run a second time?

choices.text: A hash spreads the hot key more evenly than chance
choices.why: Both spread it about as evenly.

choices.text: A retried task gets the same salts as the first try
choices.why: Right. A random salt could send a row somewhere else on the retry.

choices.text: `rand()` is not allowed inside a join
choices.why: It is allowed; the problem is that it changes.

choices.text: `rand()` cannot produce whole numbers
choices.why: Its result can be scaled and rounded.

prompt: Salting cut the largest task to under a third. Why did the job take longer?
hint: What grew eight times?

choices.text: The visitors side was copied eight times and shuffled
choices.why: Right. On this lab that cost more than the hot task did.

choices.text: Computing a hash for every event is slower than the join
choices.why: A hash per row is cheap next to a shuffle.

choices.text: The salted join gave a different answer
choices.why: The answer was the same.

choices.text: Salting disables the sort-merge join
choices.why: The plan was still a sort-merge join.

prompt: Why did adaptive execution leave this lab's hot partition alone at its default settings?
hint: Two conditions must both hold.

choices.text: Skew handling only runs on clusters of more than one machine
choices.why: It ran here once the thresholds were lowered.

choices.text: The join was a broadcast, which has no partitions to split
choices.why: Broadcasting was switched off.

choices.text: Adaptive execution only splits partitions of a `groupBy`
choices.why: It is the other way round: joins, not groupings.

choices.text: It was under 256 MB and under five times the median
choices.why: Right. 3,236 KiB against a median of 760.

prompt: After the run, the join line of the plan read `SortMergeJoin(___=true)`, which is adaptive execution saying it split a partition.
hint: The lesson's own subject, in one word.

prompt: Match each call to what it does.
hint: Only one of them avoids a shuffle.

pairs.right: Merges neighbouring partitions without a shuffle
Deals every row out in turn, into equal partitions
Puts every row of a value in one partition

right_distractors: Sorts every partition by its key

prompt: Why can `coalesce(1)` before a write be slower than `repartition(1)`?
hint: Without a shuffle, where does the stage end?

choices.text: It writes one file per input partition
choices.why: It writes one file.

choices.text: The work before it also runs as one task
choices.why: Right. No shuffle separates them, so the whole stage has one task.

choices.text: It sorts the data first
choices.why: Neither call sorts.

choices.text: It shuffles twice
choices.why: It does not shuffle at all.

prompt: A write does `repartition(50)` and then `partitionBy("day")` on 31 days, with rows of every day in every task. How many files does it write?
hint: Each task writes into every directory it has rows for.

prompt: Which writes one file per day directory?
hint: Gather each day into one task first.

choices.text: `repartition("day")`, then `partitionBy("day")`
choices.why: Right. All of a day's rows are in one task.

choices.text: `partitionBy("day")` straight after reading the input files
choices.why: A read partition can hold several days, and a day can span partitions.

choices.text: `repartition(31)`, then `partitionBy("day")`
choices.why: Rows are dealt in turn, so each task holds every day.

choices.text: `maxRecordsPerFile` set to 31
choices.why: That caps rows per file, and makes many more files.

prompt: Match each situation to the first cure to try.
hint: Ask first whether the small side fits in memory.

pairs.left: A skewed join whose small side is 30 MB
The hot key is `NULL` and no report needs those rows
pairs.right: Filter the rows out before the join

pairs.left: Two large tables, one hot customer, Spark 4 with default settings
pairs.right: Let adaptive execution split the partition

pairs.right: Repartition by the partition column first

prompt: Put the steps of salting a skewed join in order.
hint: The large side gets its salt before the small side is copied.
items: Find the hot key by counting rows per key
Add a salt from a hash to every row of the large side
Copy the small side once per salt value
Join on the key and the salt together
